padaccheda.deva: यदि मन्यसे सु वेद इति दभ्रम् एव अपि नूनम् त्वम् वेत्थ ब्रह्मणः रूपम् यत् अस्य त्वम् यत् अस्य देवेषु अथ नु मीमांस्यम् एव ते मन्ये विदितम्

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: (The teacher:) If you think ‘I know it well’, surely you know only a little of the form of Brahman: what of it you (know in yourself) and what of it (you know) among the gods. So it is still to be reflected on by you. (The pupil:) I think it is known.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: the pupil has been brought to understand ‘you, the Self, are Brahman, which is neither to be rejected nor taken up’. Lest he take this as ‘I know well that I am Brahman’, the teacher speaks to unsettle his understanding. Is not the settled understanding ‘I know it well’ what is wanted? A settled understanding is wanted, but not ‘I know it well’. What becomes an object can be known well, as what can be burnt can be burnt by fire; but fire cannot burn its own nature. The settled meaning of all the Vedānta is that Brahman is the own self of every knower; it has been taught here by ‘the ear of the ear’ (1.2), fixed in particular by 1.5, given as the conviction of the tradition in 1.4, and will be concluded in 2.3. The knower cannot be known by the knower, as fire cannot be burnt by fire; and there is no other knower for whom Brahman would be an object (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.11). So the understanding ‘I know Brahman well’ is false.

Śaṅkara: the teacher says ‘if’ with doubt, because of a thing hard to know one man, whose faults are worn away and whose mind is good, understands what he has heard, and another does not. When told ‘the person seen in the eye is the Self’ (Chāndogya 8.7.4), Virocana, king of the asuras, a son of Prajāpati and learned, took it through the fault of his nature in the opposite sense, that the body is the Self; and Indra, king of the gods, not understanding though told once, twice and thrice, understood at the fourth turn, when the fault of his nature had worn away, the Brahman taught at first. In the world too, of those who hear from one teacher one understands rightly, one not rightly, one the opposite and one not at all; how much more with the truth of the Self, which is beyond the senses, and on which all the logicians, who hold to being and to non-being, disagree.

Śaṅkara: dabhram: little. Has Brahman many forms, great and small? Yes: many, made by the adjuncts of name and form, not of itself; of itself, forms are denied together with sound and the rest (Kaṭha 1.3.15). But is not that by which a thing is marked off its own form? Consciousness is not a property of earth and the other elements, of one or of all of them transformed, nor of the senses or the inner organ; so it is the form of Brahman, and Brahman is marked off by it (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.28, 2.4.12; Taittirīya 2.1; Aitareya 3.1.3). True; yet even so it is pointed to by words such as ‘knowledge’ only through the adjuncts of inner organ, body and senses, since it seems to follow them in the growth, shrinking, cutting and perishing of the body; not of itself. Of itself it is as 2.3 will settle. ‘What of it’ goes with ‘the form of Brahman’: not only the form of Brahman limited by the adjuncts in the body, but also the form limited by the divine adjuncts, which you know among the gods, you know as little; whatever is limited by an adjunct does not cease to be small. But Brahman with every adjunct and distinction destroyed, at peace, endless, one, non-dual, called the Vast, eternal, is not a thing well known. Since this is so, I think that Brahman is still to be inquired into by you.

Śaṅkara: so addressed, the pupil sat down alone, collected; he pondered the meaning of the teaching as the teacher had given it, settled it by reasoning, made it his own experience, came back to the teacher and said: I think that Brahman is now known.

padaccheda.deva: न अहम् मन्ये सु वेद इति नो न वेद इति वेद च यः नः तत् वेद तत् वेद नो न वेद इति वेद च

translations.text: I do not think ‘I know it well’; nor (do I think) ‘I do not know’; and I know. He among us who knows that (saying) knows that (Brahman): ‘nor that I do not know; and I know’.

notes: Śaṅkara: how is it known? Hear. ‘I do not think that I know Brahman well.’ Then it is not known by you? ‘Nor that I do not know; and I know’; and by the word ‘and’, also ‘I do not know’. Is this not contradictory? If you do not think ‘I know well’, how do you think ‘I know’? That one thing is known by a man and not well known by the same man is a contradiction, unless there is doubt or error; and it cannot be laid down that Brahman is to be known as doubtful or wrongly, for doubt and error are known everywhere to do harm. Though the teacher tried in this way to unsettle him, the pupil was not unsettled, by the strength of the received teaching the teacher had given (1.4) and by the strength of reasoning and experience; and he roared, showing his own firm conviction in the knowledge of Brahman: whoever among us, fellow students, knows in truth that saying of mine knows Brahman. Which saying? ‘Nor that I do not know; and I know.’ It is the very thing said in 1.4, ‘other than the known and above the unknown’, joined with inference and experience and so made certain, which he said in another sentence, to show that his understanding agrees with the teacher's and to keep off the understanding of the dull.

words.meaning: of those who do not know

translations.text: He by whom it is not known, by him it is known; he by whom it is known does not know. It is unknown to those who know, known to those who do not know.

notes: Śaṅkara: turning from the talk of pupil and teacher, the śruti in its own person teaches what the whole talk has established. The knower of Brahman whose conviction is that Brahman is not known, by him Brahman is rightly known; he whose conviction is ‘Brahman is known by me’ does not know Brahman. The second half fixes the two positions, of the knower and of the one who does not know. ‘To those who know’: to those who have known rightly. ‘To those who do not know’: to those who do not see rightly, who see the Self in the senses, mind and understanding; not to those whose minds are wholly untaught, for they have no thought ‘Brahman is known by us’. Those who see the Self in these adjuncts do not discern Brahman from the adjunct, and the adjunct, the understanding and the rest, is known; so the error ‘Brahman is known’ can arise in them, and their wrong view is set down as the opposing side. Or the second half gives the reason for the first.

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: It is (rightly) known when it is known in each cognition, for (so) one gains immortality. By the Self one gains strength; by knowledge one gains immortality.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: it has been settled that Brahman is unknown to those who know. If it were wholly unknown, the knowers of Brahman would be no different from worldly men; and ‘unknown to those who know’ contradicts itself. How then is Brahman rightly known?

Śaṅkara: pratibodha-viditam: known with regard to cognition after cognition. bodha means the cognitions of the understanding. The Self, to which all cognitions are objects, is awake to every cognition; the seer of all cognitions, of the nature of the power of consciousness alone, it is marked by the cognitions themselves, as undistinguished in them; there is no other door to the knowledge of the inner Self. When Brahman is known as the inner self of the cognitions, that is right seeing. And as the seer of all cognitions it is established as sight that neither arises nor passes away, eternal, pure, the Self, without distinction and one in all beings, since there is no difference of mark, as with space in a jar, a mountain or a cave. So the meaning of the received teaching, that Brahman is other than the known and the unknown, is brought to its conclusion purified (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.4.2).

Śaṅkara, on other explanations: (1) If it is explained as ‘known by the mark of the act of knowing, as its agent’, as one knows wind as that which moves the branches, then the Self is a substance that has the power to know, not knowing itself; knowing arises and perishes; when it arises the Self is distinguished by it, and when it perishes the Self is bare substance: it would be changing, with parts, impermanent and impure, and these faults cannot be avoided. (2) For the followers of Kaṇāda, knowing is born of the contact of the self and the mind and inheres in the self, so that the self is a knower without changing, a bare substance like a jar in which colour inheres. Then Brahman is an unconscious substance, and the śrutis ‘Brahman is knowledge, bliss’, ‘consciousness is Brahman’ are set aside; as the self has no parts and so no places, and the mind is always joined to it, there can be no rule for the arising of memory; and that the Self has contact is against śruti and smṛti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.26; Gītā 13.14) and against reason, for what has qualities joins what has qualities and is of its kind, not what is without quality and unlike everything. So only if the Self is the knower of every cognition is it established as Brahman, the light whose nature is knowledge never lost. (3) If the sense is taken as ‘known to itself’: where the Self has adjuncts one may speak of it as knowing itself by itself, a difference being imagined through the understanding (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.23; Gītā 10.15); but the Self without adjunct, being one, can be known neither by itself nor by another, and being awareness itself needs no other awareness, as light needs no other light. On the Buddhist view of self-awareness, cognition would be momentary and without a self, against the śrutis (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.30, 4.4.25; Muṇḍaka 1.1.6). (4) Some take pratibodha as a knowing without cause, as of one who wakes from sleep, others as a knowing once for all: with cause or without, once or more than once, it is still pratibodha.

Śaṅkara: because from that knowing one gains immortality, which is deathlessness, abiding in one's own Self, liberation, it is the right view. That the knowing has the inner Self for its object is the reason for immortality: the Self's being what is not the Self is not immortality; because it is the Self, its immortality has no cause, and its mortality is only the taking of it, through ignorance, as what is not the Self. How does one gain immortality by this knowledge? By the Self, by one's own nature, one gains strength. Strength made by wealth, allies, mantras, herbs, austerity or yoga cannot overcome death, being made by impermanent things; the strength made by the knowledge of the Self is gained by the Self alone, not by anything else, and so it can overcome death. Hence by knowledge, of the Self, one gains immortality (Muṇḍaka 3.2.4).

padaccheda.deva: इह चेत् अवेदीत् अथ सत्यम् अस्ति न चेत् इह अवेदीत् महती विनष्टिः भूतेषु भूतेषु विचित्य धीराः प्रेत्य अस्मात् लोकात् अमृताः भवन्ति

translations.text: If one has known (it) here, then there is the true; if one has not known (it) here, great is the ruin. The wise, having discerned (the one Self) in being after being, turn away from this world and become immortal.

notes: Śaṅkara: hard indeed, and from ignorance, is the meeting with birth, old age, death and disease among the hosts of living beings, gods, men, animals and ghosts, full of the pain of the round of birth and death. ‘Here’: if a man, who has the claim and the ability, has known the Self as described. Then ‘there is the true’: in this human birth there is imperishableness, or meaning, or real being, or the highest truth. If, living here and having the claim, he has not known, there is great, long, endless ruin: the course of birth and death, an unbroken chain of birth, old age and death. So, knowing the gain and the loss, the wise, having discerned, known and seen directly the one truth of the Self, Brahman, in all beings, moving and unmoving, turn away from this world, which is ignorance, marked by ‘I’ and ‘mine’, and having reached oneness with the Self of all, the non-dual, become immortal, that is, become Brahman itself (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9).
